1.name: Pitot head
1.spec: Ø24 tube under the left wing at WS 3800, ram hole Ø3.2
1.note: Points into the airflow and stops it: inside, the air stands at total pressure, static plus ½ρV². At 110 kt that is about 1.97 kPa more than static.

2.name: Heater element
2.spec: 28 V, 110 W, sheathed coil inside the head
2.note: Keeps the ram hole and drain free of ice. With the heat off in cloud below freezing, ice closes the ram hole within seconds and the ASI fails.

3.name: Water dam and pressure tube
3.spec: Dam at 36 mm, tube Ø3×0.5 to the mast
3.note: Rain caught by the ram hole falls to the chamber's floor and out of the drain; air reaches the line only over the dam's top hole, so water never does.

4.name: Pitot mast and flange
4.spec: Aerofoil strut, FS 1005–1035, screwed to the wing skin
4.note: Holds the head about 90 mm below the wing, clear of the wing's own pressure field, and carries the pressure tube and the heater leads up inside it.

5.name: Pitot line
5.spec: Ø6.35×0.89, about 5.0 m, along the front spar and down the windscreen post
5.note: Carries total pressure to the ASI's capsule. Nothing flows in steady flight, so its length only adds volume: the head's holes, not the line, set how fast it responds.

6.name: Drain trap
6.spec: Clear 14 cm³ bowl at each line's lowest point
6.note: Water condensing in a line runs downhill and collects here, where it can be seen and drained, instead of plugging the line at a low point.

7.name: Static port
7.spec: Flush button, Ø2.4 hole, each side of the tail cone at FS 3000
7.note: Flush with the skin so it feels the air's pressure without its speed. It must stay clean and unpainted: a dent or a dab of polish moves every instrument.

8.name: Static lines and cross-over tee
8.spec: Ø6.35 tube and hose, the two ports teed at the cone's bottom
8.note: Joining the left and right ports averages them, so a sideslip, which raises the pressure on one side and lowers it on the other, cancels out.

9.name: Alternate static valve body
9.spec: Spool valve under the panel: ports, instruments, cabin
9.note: If both ports ice over, it lets the instruments take static pressure from the cabin instead. The cabin is a little below ambient, so they read slightly high.

10.name: Spool, O-rings and knob
10.spec: Ø10 spool, two O-rings, 9 mm pull
10.note: Pushed in, the groove joins the ports' line to the instruments; pulled, it closes the ports and opens the Ø3.2 cabin hole. Expect about +4 kt and +50 ft.

11.name: Instrument panel
11.spec: The parent's item 18, 3 mm, holes for 3⅛ in instruments
11.note: The instruments hang from it by their flanges, behind 80 mm holes on a 100 mm pitch: airspeed, attitude and altitude on top, the VSI under the altimeter.

12.name: ASI case, glass and dial
12.spec: 3⅛ in die-cast case, sealed; static fitting into the case
12.note: The case is filled with static air, the capsule with pitot air, so the capsule feels only their difference: ½ρV², the dynamic pressure.

13.name: ASI diaphragm capsule
13.spec: Ø46, two corrugated diaphragms, 1.8 mm travel at 170 kt
13.note: Swells in proportion to pitot minus static pressure. Its travel goes as V²: at 110 kt it is only about 0.6 mm, a third of its full-scale stroke.

14.name: Rocking shaft, cranks and push rod
14.spec: Crank 12 mm near dead centre, arm 12 mm
14.note: The push rod meets the crank nearly in line, so the shaft turns about as the square root of the capsule's travel: pressure becomes airspeed, and the dial can be even.

15.name: ASI sector and link
15.spec: Toothed sector, 19.6 mm pitch radius, on its own arbor
15.note: The link lifts the sector's tail; its teeth turn the pinion 10.3 times as far. A turn of 30° here carries the pointer right round the dial.

16.name: Pinion arbor and pointer
16.spec: 12-tooth pinion Ø3.8, front bridge, pointer 30 mm
16.note: The pointer sits on the pinion's arbor. The dial is the parent sheet's: 30 to 170 kt in 315°, green from 53 kt (clean stall) to 129 kt, red line at 163 kt.

17.name: Hairspring
17.note: Pulls the pinion gently one way at all times so the gear teeth always bear on the same flank: no backlash, so the pointer never jumps.

18.name: Altimeter case, glass and dial
18.spec: 3⅛ in sealed case on the static line; 100 ft a division
18.note: The whole case holds static air. Its dial is the pressure–height law of the standard atmosphere: about 27 ft for every hectopascal near sea level.

19.name: Aneroid capsule stack
19.note: Empty of air, the capsules are squeezed by the case's pressure. Climb and the pressure falls, so they swell: about 1.5 mm between sea level and 6500 ft.

20.name: Altimeter movement and cradle
20.spec: Sector 11.25:1, wheel 10:1, on a turning cradle
20.note: Two gear stages multiply the stack's small swell 112 times so the long pointer turns once per 1000 ft. The cradle turns with the baro knob.

21.name: Pointers
21.note: Long pointer hundreds, short pointer thousands, thin pointer with the triangle tens of thousands: misreading them by 10 000 ft is a classic error.

22.name: Baro knob, ring gear and scale
22.spec: Knob lower left, Kollsman scale 950–1050 hPa
22.note: Set the day's sea-level pressure (QNH) in the window and the altimeter reads height above the sea. Each hectopascal wrong is about 27 ft wrong.

23.name: VSI case, glass and dial
23.spec: 3⅛ in case, its only opening the metering unit
23.note: The case's air lags the static pressure; the capsule's does not. Zero at nine o'clock, up clockwise, ±1000 ft/min at the vertical, compressed to ±2000.

24.name: VSI diaphragm capsule
24.spec: Ø46, open to static through the fitting
24.note: In a climb static falls, the capsule's air with it at once, but the case's air is still higher: the capsule shrinks and the pointer shows the climb.

25.name: Metering unit
25.spec: Capillary Ø0.25×10 into a 300 cm³ case
25.note: The calibrated leak: Hagen–Poiseuille flow makes the case a first-order lag, τ = 8μLV/πr⁴p, about 5.5 s at sea level, so the pressure difference measures the climb rate.

26.name: VSI movement and pointer
26.spec: As the ASI's: crank, rocking shaft, sector 10.3:1, pinion, hairspring
26.note: The case lags by τ, so a steady climb holds a steady Δp = ρgwτ. The reading lags too: it needs about three τ to settle after any change.
